newsitem.title: MEXICO: Ex-Mexico president to testify in assassination probe.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Mexico president to testify in assassination probe.

text.p: Disgraced former President Carlos Salinas, in self-imposed exile in Ireland, may testify on Wednesday in the investigation into the murder of presidential candidate Luis Donaldo Colosio, newspapers said.

Salinas, who was president when his hand-picked successor was gunned down in 1994 in the border city of Tijuana, will testify at the Mexican Embassy in Dublin, leading Mexican newspapers said, citing Salinas's lawyer and unofficial sources.
"Don Carlos Salinas is going to testify either Wednesday or Thursday," La Jornada daily reported citing Salinas's lawyer Juan Velazquez.

Salinas fled Mexico in 1995 after his brother, Raul, was arrested on suspicion of ordering another political murder that rocked Mexico, that of Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, the ruling party's secretary-general.

Investigators later discovered that Raul Salinas, a high-level bureaucrat in his brother's government, had accumulated hundreds of millions of dollars that was stashed in secret European bank accounts. Raul Salinas remains in a high-security prison.

The question of whether the former president would be brought back to Mexico to make a statement in either the Colosio or Ruiz Massieu cases has been a source of wide speculation here ever since Salinas left the country.
Mexican authorities, who have hinted strongly that they would seek Salinas' version of events, officially remained tight-lipped about the probe turning to focus on Salinas.
Up to Tuesday, the attorney general's office was still refusing to confirm or deny the reports, a spokesman for Attorney General Antonio Lozano told Reuters.

Special prosecutor in the Colosio case, Luis Gonzalez Perez, travelled secretly to Ireland to interrogate Salinas, newspaper reported Tuesday. Gonzalez Perez could not be reached at his Mexico City office and officials there would not confirm his whereabouts.

Colosio almost certainly would have become president as candidate of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled Mexico for 67 years. His replacement, President Ernest Zedillo, easily won the 1994 election.

Salinas entered office in a storm of controversy in 1988 after opposition parties and some international election observers said he stole the election by fraud. But his star rose throughout his first five years on the job as he led the modernisation of Mexico's economy, making it the darling of foreign investors.

Salinas' final year, however, was a disaster marked by the political assassinations, corruption scandals and emergence of the Zapatista guerrilla force in southeastern Chiapas state. Shortly after he handed over the reins to Zedillo, the Mexican economy crashed upon the devaluation of the peso, leading to Mexico's worst recession in decades.
